title: How the CMS-HCC risk adjustment model works
questions: What is the CMS-HCC model?
How does Medicare Advantage risk adjustment predict cost?
What goes into a Medicare risk score?
Is the CMS-HCC model prospective or concurrent?
summary: The CMS-HCC model is the regression model CMS uses to estimate how costly each Medicare Advantage enrollee is expected to be relative to an average fee-for-service beneficiary. It is additive: a person's score is the sum of demographic coefficients plus a coefficient for each hierarchical condition category (HCC) their diagnoses map to, plus any disease or disability interaction terms. It is prospective, meaning diagnoses recorded in one calendar year predict spending in the following year, which is why chronic conditions must be documented again each year to keep counting. The model is calibrated on fee-for-service claims, so its coefficients reflect FFS coding patterns. Separate segments handle community versus institutional enrollees and new enrollees without a full year of diagnoses, and separate models exist for ESRD and Part D (RxHCC). Diagnoses used for payment must come from acceptable face-to-face encounters and be documented in the medical record.

facts.data_requirement: diagnoses documented in the medical record from a face-to-face visit

title: RAF score definition and how it scales MA payment
questions: What is a RAF score?
How does a risk score change what a Medicare Advantage plan is paid?
What does a risk score of 1.0 mean?
How are MA capitation payments calculated?
summary: A risk adjustment factor (RAF), or risk score, is an index of an enrollee's expected Medicare spending relative to the national fee-for-service average, which CMS keeps at roughly 1.0 through normalization. MA payment for each enrollee equals the plan's base rate for the county multiplied by that person's risk score. The base rate is the plan's standardized bid if it bids below the county benchmark, or the benchmark if it bids at or above it. A member with a score of 1.3 therefore draws about 30 percent more than the base rate, and one with 0.8 draws 20 percent less. Before payment, CMS applies the annual normalization factor and the MA coding pattern adjustment to the raw score. Plans bidding below benchmark also receive a rebate (50, 65 or 70 percent of the difference depending on star rating) that must fund extra benefits or lower premiums.

facts.payment_formula: county base rate x enrollee risk score
facts.base_rate_rule: bid if bid below benchmark, otherwise benchmark

title: HCC hierarchies: only the most severe related condition counts
questions: What is an HCC hierarchy?
If a patient has two diabetes HCCs, do both count?
How does the CMS-HCC model handle related conditions of different severity?
summary: Clinically related HCCs are arranged in hierarchies ranked by severity and cost. When a beneficiary has diagnoses mapping to more than one HCC in the same hierarchy, only the most severe one is credited and the lower ones are dropped, so payment reflects the most serious manifestation rather than stacking related codes. CMS's manual illustrates this with diabetes: if a patient's diabetes progresses to ketoacidosis during the year, the acute-complication HCC is paid and the uncomplicated-diabetes HCC is dropped. Hierarchies are republished whenever CMS recalibrates the model; the 2024 model (V28) reworked several, for example splitting heart failure into multiple severity levels and adding transplant status at the top of the heart hierarchy. For analytics, this means capturing a more specific, more severe diagnosis can replace rather than add to an existing HCC.

facts.rule: only highest-ranked HCC within a hierarchy is paid
facts.publication: hierarchies published in Rate Announcement when model is recalibrated
facts.v28_example: heart failure split into multiple HCCs; HCC 221 Heart Transplant Status/Complications added at top of hierarchy

title: Demographic factors and interaction terms in the CMS-HCC model
questions: What demographic factors are in the CMS-HCC model?
What are disease interactions in HCC risk adjustment?
Why does Medicaid or disability status change a risk score?
summary: Every MA enrollee carries a demographic component even with no diagnoses. CMS's risk adjustment manual lists five demographic factor types: age, sex, disabled status, original reason for entitlement, and Medicaid or low-income status; MedPAC adds that institutional status and being new to Medicare also matter. On top of the demographic and HCC terms, the model includes interaction terms. Disease interactions add extra weight when certain conditions co-occur because their combined cost exceeds the sum of the individual coefficients; disabled interactions add weight when particular diseases appear in beneficiaries entitled by disability. Interaction factors are simply added to the other components. Practically, this means risk scores differ for clinically similar patients depending on dual status, entitlement history and comorbidity combinations, and analytics that compare panels should account for these segments rather than HCC counts alone.

title: The FFS normalization factor
questions: What is the CMS-HCC normalization factor?
Why does CMS reduce risk scores every year?
How much did normalization lower MA payments in 2026 and 2027?
summary: Because the CMS-HCC model is calibrated on a fixed denominator year, average fee-for-service risk scores drift upward over time as the population, disease prevalence and FFS coding change. CMS offsets this with an annual normalization factor that divides risk scores so the FFS average stays near 1.0 in the payment year. The factor is estimated from the trend in FFS risk scores over recent years (traditionally a five-year window) projected forward to the payment year, and is announced in each Rate Announcement. Normalization is separate from, and applied in addition to, the MA coding pattern adjustment. For 2024 CMS set a 1.015 factor for the 2024 CMS-HCC model and excluded the COVID-affected 2021 risk scores from the trend. The combined effect of risk model revision and normalization on MA revenue was -3.01% for 2026 and -1.12% for 2027, the latter entirely from the normalization update since no new model was adopted.

facts.purpose: keep average FFS risk score at 1.0 in payment year

title: V28 (2024 CMS-HCC model): structure changes vs V24
questions: What changed in the V28 HCC model?
How many HCCs are in V28 versus V24?
How many ICD-10 codes were removed from payment HCCs in V28?
Why did CMS move to the 2024 CMS-HCC model?
summary: The 2024 CMS-HCC model, widely called V28, replaced the 2020 model (V24). CMS rebuilt the classification on ICD-10 data, recalibrated on 2018 diagnoses and 2019 expenditures, and applied its risk adjustment principles, especially Principle 10, which excludes discretionary diagnoses vulnerable to coding variation. The result classifies about 74,000 ICD-10-CM codes into 266 HCCs, 115 of them used for payment, versus 204 HCCs with 86 paid in V24. Even with more payment HCCs, the count of ICD-10 codes mapping to payment HCCs fell from 9,797 to 7,770; 2,236 codes were no longer mapped and 209 were added. CMS describes the new model as containing roughly 20 percent fewer codes. Of the 2,236 dropped codes, 2,161 (96.6%) reflected ICD-10 clinical updates and only 75 (3.4%) were Principle 10 removals aimed at discretionary coding. Because categories and denominators changed, HCC coefficients cannot be compared one-to-one across the two models.

title: V28 constrained HCCs and discretionary-code removals
questions: Which HCCs are constrained in V28?
Why are all diabetes HCCs paid the same in V28?
What is Principle 10 in CMS risk adjustment?
How did V28 treat heart failure?
summary: In building V28, CMS reviewed conditions where MA coding most exceeded FFS coding, treating that gap as a sign of discretionary coding. Using clinical input, it moved some diagnosis codes into non-payment categories, removed some categories from the payment model, and constrained related HCCs to share a single coefficient. All three diabetes payment HCCs were constrained to equal weight (V24 had constrained only the top two), so coding diabetes with chronic complications no longer pays more than uncomplicated diabetes; CMS said costs of significant complications would instead be captured by their own HCCs, such as kidney or eye disease. Heart failure was split into five HCCs to reflect severity, but the less severe split-outs were constrained together while the most severe was left unconstrained. Commenters argued constraints could discourage early identification of disease; CMS kept them.

title: V28 phase-in blend schedule, 2024-2026
questions: What was the V24/V28 blend for 2024 and 2025?
When was V28 fully phased in?
Do PACE organizations use V28?
Did MSSP and REACH follow the same V28 phase-in?
summary: CMS finalized the 2024 CMS-HCC model in the CY 2024 Rate Announcement but phased it in over three years instead of the immediate switch proposed in the Advance Notice. MA risk scores were blended 67% V24 (2020 model) and 33% V28 for 2024, 33% V24 and 67% V28 for 2025, and calculated 100% with V28 from 2026. PACE organizations are on a different track: for 2026 they used 10% of the 2024 model and 90% of the 2017 model, and for 2027 a 50/50 blend. The Shared Savings Program and ACO REACH adopted the same 67/33 blend for performance year 2024, keeping ACO benchmarks consistent with MA. For 2027 CMS proposed but did not finalize a recalibrated MA model, so V28 remains in use.

title: Estimated payment impact of V28
questions: How much did V28 cut Medicare Advantage payments?
What did MedPAC find about V28's effect on coding intensity?
Why are V28 impact estimates different?
summary: Estimates of V28's effect depend on who is measuring and what is held constant. In its CY 2024 Rate Announcement, CMS projected the new model would reduce MA payments by 3.12% if implemented at once, but by 2.16% (about $7.6 billion) with the three-year phase-in, and noted that the blend would also raise risk score trend, leaving the net first-year effect closer to -1% by one law-firm reading. MedPAC estimates V28 lowered MA coding intensity by about 2.9 percentage points in each phase-in year (2024-2026) and credits it with cutting MA's estimated payment premium over FFS from 20% (2025) to 14% (2026). MedPAC also reports plans held average rebates steady, at a record $222 per member per month in 2026, by adjusting bids. Plan-level effects vary widely with each plan's mix of affected conditions.

title: MA coding pattern difference adjustment (5.9% statutory minimum)
questions: What is the MA coding intensity adjustment?
Is the 5.9% coding adjustment still applied in 2027?
Why does the rate notice show 0% for the coding pattern adjustment?
Has CMS ever gone above the statutory minimum?
summary: Because the CMS-HCC model reflects FFS coding, MA risk scores rise faster than they would if MA enrollees were coded like FFS patients. Since 2010 CMS has reduced MA risk scores across the board to offset this; the first adjustment was 3.41%. Statute sets a minimum reduction, which reached 5.9% and has been applied every year since 2018. CMS has authority to go higher but, per MedPAC, has never done so; it applied 5.90% again for 2027 despite commenters urging tiered or plan-specific adjustments. CMS fact-sheet tables list this item as 0.00% because they show year-over-year change, not the factor itself. The reduction is uniform, so plans that code conservatively are penalized the same as aggressive coders. MedPAC estimates residual MA coding intensity remains well above 5.9% and has recommended replacing the flat factor with one that fully accounts for remaining differences.

title: MedPAC estimates of MA coding intensity (2024-2026)
questions: How much higher are MA risk scores than FFS?
What is MedPAC's estimate of excess coding in Medicare Advantage?

summary: In its March 2026 report MedPAC estimated MA risk scores were about 14% higher than for comparable FFS beneficiaries in 2024 because of coding intensity, and projected about 10% higher in 2026 as V28 finished phasing in. After CMS's 5.9% coding adjustment, MA scores remain roughly 4% above FFS-equivalent levels, worth about $22 billion of the $76 billion MedPAC attributes to MA's total payment premium in 2026. Variation is large: 16% of MA enrollees were in plans whose 2024 coding intensity fell below CMS's adjustment, eight MA organizations exceeded FFS by more than 20%, and eight of the ten largest organizations were at least 5 points above the adjustment. MedPAC also revised its earlier 2025 coding estimate downward (from 16.4% to 12.5% per a CRFB summary) using newer risk-score data. Industry groups dispute MedPAC's method, which leans on beneficiaries switching from FFS to MA.

title: MedPAC: MA paid 14% ($76B) more than FFS in 2026
questions: How much more does Medicare pay for MA enrollees than FFS?
What share of MA overpayment is favorable selection vs coding?
What did MedPAC estimate for MA spending in 2026?
summary: MedPAC projects Medicare will pay MA plans $615 billion in 2026 and estimates that is 14% (about $76 billion) more than Medicare would spend if the same beneficiaries were in FFS, down from a 20% estimate for 2025. Its decomposition: favorable selection (enrollees whose risk scores overstate their expected cost) adds about 11%, or $57 billion; coding intensity net of the 5.9% adjustment adds about $22 billion; before those two effects MA would have cost roughly $3 billion less than FFS. Quality bonuses account for about 3% ($16 billion) of MA payments. This year MedPAC folded ESRD enrollees into its estimates for the first time. MedPAC says the difference is not a measure of plan profit and varies widely across parent organizations; it recommends Congress and CMS address coding intensity, replace the quality bonus program and reform benchmarks.

title: HRAs and chart reviews drive about half of MA coding intensity
questions: How much do health risk assessments add to MA payments?
What share of coding intensity comes from chart reviews?
How many HCCs are found only on HRAs or chart reviews?
summary: MedPAC analyzed 2022 encounter data to isolate diagnoses supported only by a health risk assessment (HRA) or a plan chart review, with no other physician or hospital service for that condition in the year. About 7.7 million MA enrollees had an HRA that identified at least one HCC; 5.7 million HCCs (a third of HRA-identified HCCs) appeared only on an HRA, generating about $15 billion in 2023 payments, roughly 3% of MA payments. About 80% of those HRA-only dollars came from HRAs done during annual wellness visits or initial preventive exams, the rest from in-home HRAs. Chart reviews identified 33.2 million HCCs for 12 million enrollees; 9.0 million (about 27%) appeared only on chart reviews. Together, HRAs and chart reviews accounted for about $34 billion, about 8% of 2023 MA payments, which MedPAC concludes is roughly half of all MA coding intensity.

title: OIG 2024: HRA-only diagnoses drove $7.5B in MA payments
questions: What did OIG find about in-home health risk assessments?
How much MA payment came from diagnoses only on HRAs?
Which MA companies drove HRA-based payments?
summary: HHS OIG's October 2024 evaluation (OEI-03-23-00380) examined diagnoses reported only on health risk assessments or on chart reviews linked to HRAs, with no other 2022 service record for the condition. Those diagnoses generated an estimated $7.5 billion in 2023 MA risk-adjusted payments for about 1.7 million enrollees. Almost two-thirds of that amount came from in-home HRAs and their linked chart reviews, and just 20 MA companies drove 80% of the payments. OIG noted the absence of follow-up visits, tests or treatment means either the diagnoses are inaccurate, making the payments improper, or enrollees did not get needed care. It recommended CMS restrict use of diagnoses reported only on in-home HRAs or linked chart reviews, audit them, and assess which HCCs are prone to misuse; diabetes and heart failure were cited as examples.

title: OIG 2021: chart reviews and HRAs concentrated in a few MA companies
questions: What did OIG's 2021 report on chart reviews find?
Did OIG find one MA company drove chart review payments?
summary: In September 2021, HHS OIG (OEI-03-17-00474) reported that a subset of MA companies leveraged chart reviews and health risk assessments to generate a disproportionate share of risk-adjusted payments from those sources. OIG recommended CMS provide oversight of the 20 companies with disproportionate shares and review whether the one company that substantially drove these payments was paid appropriately and whether its enrollees received appropriate care. OIG did not conclude any company acted improperly. This report is the precursor to OIG's 2024 HRA-focused evaluation and to MedPAC's later quantification of chart-review and HRA effects. For VBC analytics teams, it is a reminder that diagnosis capture concentrated in retrospective review or HRA channels, without linked treatment, draws regulatory scrutiny.

title: CY 2027: unlinked chart reviews and audio-only diagnoses excluded
questions: Are unlinked chart review diagnoses used for risk adjustment in 2027?
What changed in the 2027 MA Rate Announcement for risk adjustment?
Are audio-only telehealth diagnoses risk-adjustable?

summary: The CY 2027 Rate Announcement (April 6, 2026) finalized two diagnosis-source restrictions for MA risk scores. First, diagnoses from audio-only services (modifiers 93 or FQ) are excluded. Second, diagnoses from unlinked chart review records, meaning plan chart reviews not tied to an actual encounter record, are excluded, with an exception for beneficiaries who switch MA organizations; plans may still submit them but they will not count. CMS estimated the unlinked-CRR exclusion lowers MA risk scores 1.53% on average (1.78% without the switcher exception) and the audio-only exclusion about 0%. CMS did not adopt the proposed recalibrated MA model and keeps the 2024 CMS-HCC model. Overall, CMS projected a 2.48% average payment increase (over $13 billion), or 4.98% including a 2.50% expected risk score trend. The PACE exclusion does not apply to unlinked CRRs for 2027.

summary: The CY 2026 Rate Announcement completed the V28 transition: MA risk scores for 2026 are calculated entirely with the 2024 CMS-HCC model, while PACE used a 10/90 blend of the 2024 and 2017 models. title: Annual recapture and chronic condition documentation
questions: Why do chronic conditions need to be documented every year?
What is HCC recapture?
What documentation supports a risk-adjustable diagnosis?
What is suspecting in risk adjustment?
summary: Because the CMS-HCC model is prospective and uses each calendar year's diagnoses to set the next year's score, a chronic condition counts only if it is documented again during the year. Analytics teams call this recapture: tracking which previously documented HCCs have not yet been re-captured and prompting a visit. Suspecting extends this to conditions implied by data such as labs, medications or prior history but never coded. CMS requires that submitted diagnoses come from an acceptable face-to-face encounter, be documented in the medical record, and follow ICD-10-CM coding guidelines; RADV audits test exactly that. AAFP guidance stresses documenting the current status of each chronic condition reported rather than carrying forward problem lists. Regulators distinguish legitimate recapture tied to care from add-on coding without treatment, which OIG and MedPAC flag in HRA and chart-review analyses.

facts.basis: prospective model; each year's diagnoses set next year's score

title: Annual wellness visits, HRAs and diagnosis capture
questions: How do annual wellness visits affect risk scores?
Are in-home health risk assessments allowed for risk adjustment?
What share of HRA-only payments comes from wellness visits?
summary: Annual wellness visits (AWVs) and initial preventive physical exams include a health risk assessment, and diagnoses documented at those visits can enter MA risk scores. MedPAC found that about 80% of 2023 MA payments generated by diagnoses found only on HRAs came from HRAs done during AWVs or initial preventive exams, with the remainder from in-home HRAs. OIG, focusing on in-home HRAs and linked chart reviews, found they produced almost two-thirds of $7.5 billion in HRA-only payments and urged CMS to restrict their use. MedPAC has recommended excluding diagnoses documented only on HRAs, from both MA and FFS, as part of a broader coding-adjustment overhaul. For provider groups in risk arrangements, AWVs remain a legitimate venue to assess and document conditions, but diagnoses with no linked follow-up care are the most exposed to future policy and audit.

title: RADV final rule (2023): extrapolation from PY2018, no FFS adjuster
questions: What is a RADV audit?
What did the 2023 RADV final rule change?
What is the FFS adjuster and was it dropped?
From which payment year can CMS extrapolate RADV findings?
summary: Risk Adjustment Data Validation (RADV) audits check whether diagnoses an MA organization submitted for payment are supported by enrollees' medical records; unsupported codes become overpayments. CMS's final rule released January 30, 2023 (CMS-4185-F2) made two major choices. CMS will extrapolate audit error rates from the sampled enrollees to the whole contract starting with payment year 2018, while for PY 2011-2017 it collects only the specific overpayments found in sampled records (it had proposed extrapolating from 2011). It also declined to apply a fee-for-service adjuster, an offset plans argued was needed because FFS claims data also contain unsupported diagnoses; CMS said actuarial equivalence governs how payments are risk adjusted, not the duty to repay unsupported codes. CMS did not prescribe a single sampling method, relying on any statistically valid approach. A federal court later vacated the rule (see RADV litigation entry).

How many records per contract do RADV audits sample now?
How big are MA improper payments from unsupported diagnoses?

summary: On May 21, 2025 CMS announced it would audit all eligible MA contracts for each payment year, versus roughly 60 contracts a year previously (about 30 per year for PYs 2011-2013), and accelerate completion of PY 2018-2024 audits by early 2026. CMS's July 2025 fast-facts sheet says audits for PY 2019 onward include all RADV-eligible contracts, sample sizes rise from 35 enrollees per contract to 35-200 starting with PY 2020, and extrapolation applies from PY 2018. Per a Proskauer summary, CMS planned to grow its coder workforce from about 40 to about 2,000 by September 2025 and use enhanced technology to flag unsupported diagnoses. CMS cites the Part C improper payment measure for PY 2022: a 5.06% overpayment error rate, $17.2 billion overpaid, with 84.54% of improper payments tied to medical record discrepancies, and estimates unsupported diagnoses cost about $17 billion a year.

title: RADV rule vacated in 2025 (Humana v. Becerra); status of extrapolation
questions: Was the RADV extrapolation rule struck down?
Can CMS still extrapolate RADV findings?
What are the PY2020 RADV audit dates?
summary: CMS's PY 2020 RADV audit instructions (March 20, 2026) state that the 2023 RADV rule on sampling and extrapolation was vacated by a federal district court in 2025, in Humana Inc. v. Becerra (N.D. Tex.), and that the decision is under appeal. CMS nonetheless designed the PY 2020 contract-level audits to support extrapolated recoveries and says it will decide later whether to extrapolate or recover only sampled enrollees' overpayments. Contracts are stratified, with samples of 200, 100, 50 or 35 enrollees by stratum. Key PY 2020 dates: enrollee data lists available April 3, 2026; medical record submission window April 13 to August 28, 2026; hardship requests due September 11, 2026. For plans and risk-bearing providers, the practical exposure from extrapolation therefore depends on the appeal outcome, while sample-level recoveries proceed regardless.

title: MSSP benchmark risk adjustment and the 3% cap

summary: MSSP adjusts an ACO's historical benchmark for changes in its assigned beneficiaries' prospective CMS-HCC risk scores between the third benchmark year and each performance year, but limits upward movement to 3% over the agreement period. The CY 2023 PFS final rule changed how the cap works for agreement periods starting January 1, 2024 or later: demographic risk score growth is accounted for first, and the cap is applied in aggregate across the four enrollment types (ESRD, disabled, aged/dual, aged/non-dual) rather than to each separately. The CY 2024 rule added a cap on prospective HCC risk score growth in the ACO's regional service area that accounts for market share, and required using the performance-year CMS-HCC model for all benchmark years, phasing in V28 at 67% V24/33% V28 for 2024. title: ACO REACH risk adjustment: CIF, symmetric caps, concurrent model
questions: How does ACO REACH risk adjust?
What is the REACH coding intensity factor?
What risk model do High Needs REACH ACOs use?

summary: ACO REACH normalizes beneficiary risk scores, applies an ACO-level symmetric cap on risk score growth, and then applies a retrospective, zero-sum, model-wide coding intensity factor (CIF) so average risk scores do not grow relative to a reference year. For PY 2024, Standard and New Entrant ACOs used the MA model blend (67% V24, 33% V28) with a 3% symmetric cap measured against a static reference year with demographic adjustment, and the CIF was limited to no more than 1%. High Needs Population ACOs use a concurrent CMMI-HCC model, which predicts same-year cost from same-year diagnoses, with a 10% symmetric cap and the same CIF limit. The Kidney Care Choices CKCC options use prospective CMS-HCC and ESRD models with entity-level caps (plus or minus 3% for ESRD and 6% for CKD 4-5 scores) but no CIF.

title: HHS-HCC risk adjustment in the ACA individual and small group markets
questions: How does ACA marketplace risk adjustment work?

summary: The ACA created a permanent risk adjustment program for the individual and small group markets that moves money within each state market risk pool from issuers with lower-than-average enrollee risk to issuers with higher-than-average risk; it is not a payment from the government. HHS has operated it in all 50 states and DC since 2017. The methodology accounts for enrollee actuarial risk (via the HHS-HCC model, which since 2018 also uses certain prescription drug classes for adults), plan actuarial value, local cost of doing business and induced utilization from cost-sharing. Since 2018 statewide average premiums in the transfer formula are cut 14% for administrative costs, and a high-cost risk pool reimburses part of very expensive claims. For benefit year 2025, 557 issuers participated, and transfers equaled about 9.0% of premiums nationally (11.0% individual, 3.9% small group).

title: CDPS+Rx: Medicaid managed care risk adjustment

summary: Many state Medicaid programs risk adjust managed care capitation using the Chronic Illness and Disability Payment System (CDPS), developed at UC San Diego. CDPS is diagnosis-based: ICD codes map to categories reflecting illness burden, with additive weights across major body systems or chronic disease types. The companion Medicaid Rx (MRX) model uses pharmacy NDC codes to assign medication-therapy categories, and CDPS+Rx combines both. Scores are calculated per person but applied at the health-plan group level. The model has been recalibrated over time; the 7.0 update drew on three national Medicaid managed care plans, and published R-squared values for version 7.2 are substantially higher for concurrent than prospective versions (for adults, 0.37 versus 0.14). Unlike Medicare, Medicaid populations are segmented by eligibility group such as disabled, children and adults.

title: Medicare Advantage Star Ratings: structure and timing
questions: How do Medicare Advantage Star Ratings work?
How many measures are in the MA Star Ratings?
When are Star Ratings released and which payment year do they affect?
summary: CMS rates MA and Part D contracts from 1 to 5 stars, in half-star increments, to inform beneficiaries and determine quality bonus payments. For the 2027 Star Ratings, released October 8, 2026, MA-PD contracts are rated on up to 43 measures, MA-only contracts on up to 32, and stand-alone PDPs on up to 13. Each measure is converted to stars using cut points recalculated every year. Measure stars roll up into domain ratings (unweighted means), Part C and Part D summary ratings, and an overall rating that is a weighted average of measure stars, plus a reward factor and a Categorical Adjustment Index. Data come from HEDIS, CAHPS, the Health Outcomes Survey, Part D prescription data and CMS administrative sources, mostly from a measurement year two years before the rating year. The 2027 ratings appear on Medicare Plan Finder for the 2027 open enrollment and set 2028 quality bonus payments.

title: How Star cut points are set: clustering, Tukey outlier deletion, guardrails
questions: How does CMS set Star Ratings cut points?
What is Tukey outlier deletion in Star Ratings?
What are cut point guardrails?
How are CAHPS star thresholds determined?
summary: For non-CAHPS measures CMS sets cut points with hierarchical clustering of contract scores. Before clustering, it removes Tukey outer-fence outliers, scores more than 3.0 times the interquartile range below the first quartile or above the third. It then uses mean resampling: scores are split into 10 groups, clustering runs 10 times leaving one group out, and the 10 sets of cut points are averaged. Guardrails cap each cut point's change from the prior year to 5 percentage points for 0-100 scale measures, or 5% of the prior year's restricted range otherwise. CAHPS measures use a different method combining percentile rank with significance testing: 5 stars requires at least the 80th percentile and a score significantly above the national average (with reliability conditions); 1 star requires being below the 15th percentile and significantly below average. Because cut points move yearly, a plan can lose stars with unchanged performance.

facts.guardrail_cap: 5 percentage points (0-100 scale) or 5% of restricted range

facts.cahps_1_star: <15th percentile and significantly below national average

title: Reward factor and the Health Equity Index transition
questions: What is the Star Ratings reward factor?
Did the Health Equity Index replace the reward factor?
How much can the reward factor add to a Star Rating?
summary: The reward factor (r-Factor) adds up to 0.4 stars to summary and overall ratings for contracts that perform consistently well. CMS computes each contract's weighted mean and weighted variance of measure stars, then awards 0.4 for low variance with a mean at or above the 85th percentile, 0.3 for medium variance and high mean, 0.2 for low variance with a mean from the 65th to 85th percentile, 0.1 for medium variance in that band, and 0 otherwise. In its April 2023 final rule (CMS-4201-F), CMS finalized a Health Equity Index (HEI) reward beginning with the 2027 Star Ratings to reward performance for enrollees with social risk factors, intended to replace the reward factor. However, the 2027 Technical Notes published September 30, 2026 still describe and apply the reward factor and contain no HEI calculation. Users should check the current year's Technical Notes before modeling either reward.

title: Categorical Adjustment Index (CAI)
questions: What is the Categorical Adjustment Index in Star Ratings?
Do Star Ratings adjust for dual eligibles?
How does CMS account for low-income members in Star Ratings?
summary: The Categorical Adjustment Index is an add-on or deduction to a contract's summary and overall Star Ratings that offsets the average within-contract performance gap for beneficiaries who are low-income subsidy recipients or dual eligible (LIS/DE) and those with disability status. The CAI value depends on the contract's share of LIS/DE and disabled enrollees. CMS derives it by case-mix adjusting clinical measure scores that are not already adjusted for socioeconomic status, using a beneficiary-level logistic regression with contract fixed effects and only LIS/DE and disability as adjusters, converting adjusted scores to stars, and comparing adjusted with unadjusted ratings. For the 2027 ratings the CAI uses data collected for the 2026 Star Ratings. It is applied both with and without improvement measures. For plans heavy in duals, the CAI partly compensates for social risk but does not remove it from measure-level results.

title: MA quality bonus payments: 4+ stars raise benchmarks

summary: MA contracts with an overall rating of 4 stars or higher receive a quality bonus that raises their county benchmarks by 5 percentage points, or 10 points in qualifying double-bonus counties (urban areas with low FFS spending and historically high managed care enrollment), subject to benchmark caps. Star ratings also set the share of savings below benchmark a plan keeps as rebates (50%, 65% or 70%). Unlike most FFS quality programs, the bonuses are not budget neutral; MedPAC estimates they add about $16 billion, roughly 3% of MA payments, in 2026. Forty percent of rated contracts are in bonus status for 2026 (down from 44% in 2024), covering a projected 64% of enrollees. Ratings released in October of one year set bonuses two years later; the 2027 Star Ratings determine 2028 QBPs. MedPAC has repeatedly recommended replacing the program with a budget-neutral alternative.

title: HEDIS: what it is and how widely it is used
questions: What is HEDIS?
How many HEDIS measures are there?
Who reports HEDIS?
What are the HEDIS domains?
summary: HEDIS (Healthcare Effectiveness Data and Information Set) is NCQA's standardized performance measurement set for health plans. NCQA describes it as one of health care's most widely used performance improvement tools, with more than 90 measures across six domains: effectiveness of care, access/availability of care, experience of care, utilization and risk-adjusted utilization, health plan descriptive information, and measures reported using electronic clinical data systems. More than 235 million people are enrolled in plans that report HEDIS. Results are audited by NCQA-certified auditors before public reporting. HEDIS measures feed Medicare Star Ratings (for example breast and colorectal cancer screening, blood pressure control and glycemic status), Medicaid managed care quality programs and many commercial value-based contracts, so provider groups in VBC arrangements are usually measured on HEDIS specifications even when the contract is with a plan rather than CMS.

title: HEDIS ECDS transition and retirement of the hybrid method
questions: What is HEDIS ECDS reporting?
When will NCQA retire the HEDIS hybrid method?
Which HEDIS measures are ECDS-only?
What is the difference between hybrid and administrative HEDIS?
summary: HEDIS measures have historically been reported administratively (from claims and encounters) or by the hybrid method, which supplements administrative data with medical record review of a sample. NCQA is moving measures to Electronic Clinical Data Systems (ECDS) reporting, a standard for plans to collect and submit electronic clinical data from four source categories: EHR/personal health records, HIEs and clinical registries, case management systems, and administrative data. Measures moved to ECDS-only reporting on a schedule: Breast Cancer Screening in MY 2023; Colorectal Cancer Screening and two pediatric behavioral health measures in MY 2024; childhood and adolescent immunizations and cervical cancer screening in MY 2025; lead screening and the two statin therapy measures in MY 2026. NCQA plans to remove the hybrid method by MY 2029. Source system of record reporting is no longer required as of MY 2026. For providers, data interoperability with plans increasingly determines measured performance.

title: MSSP quality performance standard and alternative standard

summary: MSSP links shared savings to quality through a quality performance standard. An ACO meets it, and can share savings at its track's maximum rate (and, in ENHANCED, avoid maximum losses), by scoring at or above the 40th percentile of all MIPS quality performance category scores. Since PY 2024 that percentile is a rolling three-year average with a one-year lag: 76.70 for PY 2025 and 73.85 for PY 2026 (average of 77.73, 74.54 and 69.27 from PY 2022-2024). ACOs reporting all five eCQM/MIPS CQMs with complete data can instead meet the eCQM reporting incentive: 10th percentile on one of four outcome measures and 40th percentile on one other measure. First-year ACOs meet it by complete reporting. Under the alternative standard, introduced in PY 2023, ACOs hitting the 10th percentile on one outcome measure share savings at a rate scaled by their quality score; ACOs that report nothing get no savings.

summary: The CY 2023 PFS final rule created a health equity adjustment for Shared Savings Program ACOs that report all-payer eCQMs or MIPS CQMs. It adds up to 10 bonus points to the ACO's MIPS quality performance category score, based on high quality performance combined with the proportion of assigned beneficiaries who are underserved, identified using the Area Deprivation Index, Part D low-income subsidy enrollment and dual eligibility. The adjustment can only add points. The CY 2024 rule refined the underserved multiplier to count beneficiaries with partial-year LIS or dual status and removed beneficiaries lacking a national ADI rank, and applied the adjustment to the MIPS quality score used to calculate shared savings. Whether the adjustment continues in later performance years should be checked against the most recent PFS rule; current-year status was not confirmed from a retrieved source.

title: ACO REACH quality measures and quality withhold
questions: What quality measures does ACO REACH use?
How big is the REACH quality withhold?
What is Days at Home in ACO REACH?
How does the REACH total quality score work?
summary: ACO REACH holds back part of each ACO's financial benchmark as a quality withhold that ACOs earn back based on a Total Quality Score. Measures are all-condition readmission (ACR) and all-cause unplanned admissions for patients with multiple chronic conditions (UAMCC) for every ACO type, timely follow-up after acute exacerbations of chronic conditions (TFU) for Standard and New Entrant ACOs, Days at Home (DAH) for High Needs Population ACOs, and the CAHPS survey. The withhold was 5% in PY 2021-2022 (mostly pay-for-reporting), dropped to 2% fully pay-for-performance for PY 2023-2025, and returns to 5% for PY 2026. From PY 2024 the four measures are equally weighted, so in PY 2026 each governs up to 1.25% of benchmark. Bonus adjustments reward continuous improvement or sustained exceptional performance, and a High Performers Pool pays extra. REACH runs through PY 2026.

title: ACO REACH PY 2024 quality and financial results
questions: How did ACO REACH perform in 2024?
What was the average REACH total quality score?
How much did REACH save Medicare in PY 2024?
summary: CMS released PY 2024 ACO REACH results on July 9, 2026. Across 115 ACOs, the average Total Quality Score was 80.4% for 101 Standard and New Entrant ACOs and 86.2% for 14 High Needs ACOs; 21 ACOs scored 100%. Most (101 of 115) met continuous improvement or sustained exceptional performance criteria, and 49 qualified for the High Performers Pool. Timely follow-up improved 5.7 points and Days at Home 3.58 points from PY 2023. Financially, REACH ACOs generated about $2.511 billion gross savings (6.7% versus adjusted benchmarks), with $988.3 million net to CMS and $1.522 billion to ACOs; 96 ACOs earned savings. Ninety-five percent of CMS's net savings came from the 3% discount on Global-option benchmarks. CMS notes these benchmark-based results differ from, and are typically less conservative than, the independent evaluation.

title: Medicaid and CHIP Core Sets: mandatory reporting from 2024
questions: Is Medicaid Core Set reporting mandatory?
What are the Child and Adult Core Sets?
When did mandatory Medicaid quality reporting start?
summary: CMS maintains standardized quality measure sets for Medicaid and CHIP: the Child Core Set and the Adult Core Set. Reporting was voluntary for years, but beginning in 2024 reporting of the Child Core Set and the behavioral health measures in the Adult Core Set became mandatory for all states, the District of Columbia and the territories named by CMS, under regulations at 42 CFR Parts 433, 437 and 457 finalized in a Core Set rule published August 31, 2023. CMS issues annual updates to the sets through State Health Official letters and publicly reports measures reported by at least 25 states. For VBC organizations serving Medicaid populations, Core Set measures are the measures states are most likely to embed in managed care contracts and directed-payment quality programs, and many overlap with HEDIS and the CMS Universal Foundation.

title: CMS Universal Foundation measures
questions: What is the CMS Universal Foundation?
Which measures are in the Universal Foundation?
How is CMS aligning quality measures across programs?
summary: The Universal Foundation is CMS's core set of high-priority quality measures meant to be used across its programs so that clinicians and plans face fewer, more consistent measures, with emphasis on prevention, wellness and chronic disease management. For adults, CMS lists colorectal and breast cancer screening, adult immunization status, controlling high blood pressure, HbA1c poor control (>9%), depression screening and follow-up, initiation and engagement of substance use disorder treatment, all-cause readmissions, and CAHPS overall ratings. Pediatric measures add well-child visits, immunizations, weight assessment, oral evaluation, asthma medication ratio, and several behavioral health follow-up measures. Domains are wellness and prevention, chronic conditions, behavioral health, seamless care coordination, person-centered care and safety, with add-on measures for hospital, post-acute and maternity settings. The MSSP Medicare CQM collection type and APP Plus set were explicitly designed to align with it.

title: MedPAC critique of the MA quality bonus program
questions: Why does MedPAC want to replace MA quality bonuses?
Do Star Ratings reflect real quality differences?
How many MA contracts get quality bonuses?
summary: MedPAC argues the MA quality bonus program spends heavily without reliably distinguishing plan quality. Its March 2026 report estimates bonuses add about $16 billion to 2026 MA payments, financed by program dollars and beneficiary premiums rather than budget neutrally, unlike nearly all FFS quality incentive programs. Forty percent of rated contracts are in bonus status for 2026 and 64% of enrollees are projected to be in bonus contracts, with an average star rating of 3.98 by MedPAC's count. The Commission has repeatedly recommended replacing the system with a budget-neutral program that scores a small set of population-based measures, evaluates quality at the local-market level, uses peer grouping to account for enrollees' social risk, and avoids cliff effects. It notes contracts can span wide geographic areas, blurring what a rating describes. Plans and industry groups generally defend Star Ratings as a driver of quality improvement; no industry rebuttal was retrieved here.

facts.recommendation: replace with budget-neutral quality incentive program
